q: A team's chatbot gives outdated pricing. Which first step best fits the cost ladder?
options: Fine-tune on the pricing page weekly
Retrieve current pricing at request time or call a pricing tool
Train a larger model from scratch
why: Pricing is changing knowledge; retrieval or a tool keeps it current and cites it. Weekly tuning is costly and still goes stale.

q: Which failure bucket is the strongest candidate for fine-tuning?
options: Answers lacking facts from internal documents
Inconsistent brand tone that prompts only partially fix
Context window overflow on long files
why: Tone/style is behaviour that tuning can bake in. The others are retrieval, chunking or access-control problems.

q: What is the most durable asset in a fine-tuning project when the base model is deprecated?
options: The versioned dataset, recipe and eval suite
why: Adapters are bound to the old base; data, scripts and evals let you retrain quickly on a successor.

q: Which cost is typically underestimated when proposing a tune?
options: Data curation, evals and ongoing maintenance
why: People time on data and evals plus retraining and hosting usually dominates a cheap training run.

q: Training loss is low but the served model never stops generating. Most likely cause?
options: Missing end-of-turn token or different template at train time
why: A template/EOS mismatch teaches or serves the wrong stop pattern. Rank and data size would not specifically cause endless generation.

q: Why mask prompt tokens in the SFT loss?
options: So gradients focus on the response the model must produce
To avoid needing a chat template
why: Prompts are inputs at inference; training on them wastes capacity and dilutes the response signal when prompts are long.

q: A tune scores 98% on test but fails in production. What do you suspect first?
options: Leakage between train and test via duplicates or shared sources
why: Unrealistically high test scores point to leaked near-duplicates; re-split by group and test on fresh traffic.

q: You have 300 expert examples and need broader coverage. Best approach?
options: Use them as seeds for teacher-generated variants, filtered and spot-checked, keeping a real held-out set
why: Seeded synthetic expansion with filtering adds diversity; duplication adds none and a real held-out set keeps evaluation honest.

q: After cleaning, aggregate accuracy rose but hard-case accuracy fell. Why?
why: Aggressive filters can strip difficult cases, skewing toward easy data; compare per-category counts before and after.

q: Validation loss rises while train loss keeps falling. Best action?
options: Stop earlier or select an earlier checkpoint and reduce LR/epochs
why: This is overfitting; earlier checkpoint and fewer epochs help. More epochs worsens it.

q: Which statement about SFT is most accurate?
options: It reliably teaches large amounts of new factual knowledge
It shifts behaviour toward demonstrations and is capped by data quality
why: SFT imitates demonstrations; it changes style and mapping more than knowledge, and flawed data is imitated too.

q: After tuning, the model refuses fewer unsafe requests. What is this an example of?
why: Narrow tuning eroded earlier abilities including safety; add safety data and a regression suite.

q: Which setup best selects a checkpoint?
options: Evaluate saved checkpoints on validation task metrics and regressions, confirm on test once
why: Task evals, selected on validation and confirmed on a frozen test, avoid overfit and selection bias.

q: Why is QLoRA useful?
options: It holds the frozen base in 4-bit so larger models fit on small GPUs while training LoRA adapters
It removes the need for data
why: Quantizing the frozen base saves memory; adapters still train in higher precision.

q: LoRA underfits a hard task with adapters on q and v only at rank 4. First change?
options: Add MLP projections to targets and/or raise rank
why: More capacity (more target layers or rank) addresses underfitting; lower rank worsens it.

q: 50 tenants each need a tuned variant on the same base. Best design?
options: One prompt per tenant only, no serving changes needed
One LoRA per tenant with multi-adapter serving on a shared base
why: Small swappable adapters share one base, which is far cheaper than full copies.

q: A QLoRA job OOMs only on long examples. Most likely reason?
options: Activation memory scales with sequence length
why: Activations scale with batch x length; use checkpointing, shorter length or smaller micro-batches.

q: A client's data cannot leave their network. Which route?
options: DIY tuning with an open-weight base inside their environment
why: Managed tuning moves data out of the boundary; DIY keeps it in.

q: Why run SFT before DPO?
options: SFT puts the model on-distribution so pairs are on-policy and the reference is sensible
SFT replaces the need for a reference model
DPO needs a reward model first
why: Without SFT, chosen and rejected answers are off-distribution and the anchor is weak.

q: Win rate improved 15 points but responses doubled in length. Best reading?
options: Likely length bias exploited by judges or raters; control for length
why: Raters and judges favour long answers; use length-controlled comparison.

q: Which failure is NOT a good target for DPO?
why: Format errors are fixed by SFT or constrained decoding; DPO refines among valid answers.

q: In DPO what does a higher beta do?
options: Lets the policy drift further from the reference
Keeps the policy closer to the reference
why: Beta scales the penalty for diverging from the reference, so higher means more conservative.

q: You have unit tests but no demonstration solutions. Which method?
options: RFT with tests as the reward
why: Tests provide a reward; no demonstrations or pairs are required.

q: Training reward rises, held-out eval is flat. What is likely?
why: The model exploits grader flaws; audit high-reward samples and add independent checks.

q: The base model scores 0% pass rate. What is the problem for RFT?
options: No reward variance, so nothing to reinforce
why: If no sample succeeds there is no signal; warm up with SFT or simplify the task.

q: A student is evaluated only against the teacher's labels. What is wrong?
options: It measures imitation including teacher mistakes, not true accuracy
The student will be too large
why: Use human-labelled held-out data to measure real quality.

q: Which is a risk of repeated synthetic-on-synthetic training?
why: Tails of the distribution vanish when models train on their own outputs without fresh real data.

q: The teacher's terms forbid training competing models. Best action?
options: Ignore it since outputs are public
Hide the origin of the data
Choose a permissively licensed teacher or human data and consult legal
why: Terms are a legal constraint; use permitted sources.

q: Which design captures savings while protecting quality?
options: Route low-confidence student outputs to the teacher
why: A confidence-based fallback keeps most traffic cheap and hard cases accurate.

q: A tune beats a one-line prompt baseline by 20 points. Best response?
options: Compare against a well-engineered prompt with few-shot and retrieval before judging
why: A weak baseline overstates the tune's benefit.

q: Aggregate accuracy is +3 but the payments slice is down 8. What should happen?
options: Block or fix: critical slice regression outweighs the average
why: Slice analysis exposes harm hidden by averages.

q: The judge used for evaluation is the same model that generated the training data. Issue?
options: Self-preference bias can inflate the tune's score
why: Use a different, human-calibrated judge.

q: After error analysis, a refined prompt nearly matches the tune's score. Best move?
options: Prefer the prompt unless the tune's remaining gain justifies its maintenance
why: Simpler options win when the gain is small relative to ongoing cost.

q: You serve 30 tenant-specific tunes on one base. Best deployment?
why: Adapters share the base, and batching across them keeps GPUs efficient.

q: Why merge LoRA into a 16-bit base before quantizing for GGUF?
options: Merging into already quantized weights adds rounding error
Quantized bases cannot load adapters ever
why: Merge in high precision, then quantize once.

q: A tune works in a notebook but rambles in production. First suspicion?
options: Chat template or stop tokens differ between training and serving
why: Template/EOS mismatch is the classic cause.

q: What makes rollback fast?
options: Overwriting the adapter file in place
Immutable versions served via an alias you can repoint
why: Aliases make rollback a pointer change to a retained version.

q: What is a sound rollout path for a new adapter?
options: Test on the training set only
Shadow, then small canary against baseline control, then ramp with abort thresholds
Release to the largest customer first
why: Staged rollout limits blast radius and compares against a control.

q: A hiring manager asks you to fine-tune their FAQ bot on the company wiki. Best refusal?
options: Refuse: changing facts need retrieval and citations; tune only a leftover style gap after that
Train from scratch on the wiki dump
why: FAQs go stale and need citations and ACLs. That is RAG. A tune that bakes the wiki will be confidently wrong next quarter.

q: Which line belongs in the first cost estimate, not only the GPU invoice?
options: The next base-model retrain tax, plus data and evals
The colour of the W&B chart
why: Adapters die when the base is deprecated. If you omit retrains, data and evals you underquoted the project.

q: A random 80/20 split on raw tickets later shows near-duplicate prompts in train and test. What was missing?
options: A leak scan that hashes normalised prompts and paraphrases
why: Exact-string dedup misses paraphrases. Leakage inflates the headline. Hash and near-dup before you believe the score.

q: Every dataset version gets a 50-row hand audit. Error rate is 8%. Next step?
options: Stop training and fix labels or the spec; do not launch the job
why: An 8% gold error rate means you would train against a dirty exam. The audit is a gate, not a souvenir.

q: Train loss is still falling but the task metric has been flat for two evals and refusals are worse. What do you keep?
options: The last step because loss is lowest
The checkpoint that won the skill without tripping the forgetting/safety gate
why: Pick by the skill and the kill criteria, not by the last epoch or the lowest train loss. Loss can fall by memorising phrasing.

q: You have not yet swept learning rate but you are already sweeping rank, alpha and epochs. What first?
options: A small learning-rate grid at fixed architecture
why: A diverging LR makes every other sweep noise. Three LRs on morning one beats two days of rank theatre.

q: A 4-bit QLoRA train looked great. The 4-bit served file drops schema validity 4 points. Lesson?
options: A 4-bit train does not guarantee a 4-bit serve win; re-eval after merge and requant
why: Merge on higher precision, then quantise for serve, and score that artefact. Train loss is not a serve certificate.

q: You serve 20 tenant tones. Merge every adapter into its own full checkpoint?
options: No — keep separate adapters on one shared base (multi-LoRA)
why: Twenty merged copies are twenty full models. Separate adapters share the base and stay swappable. Keep the unmerged files either way.

q: Preferred answers are systematically longer than rejected ones. What will DPO likely learn?
options: Length, unless you length-match or penalise it
why: Uncontrolled length bias teaches rambling. Histograms of preferred vs rejected belong on the data card.

q: When do you ship DPO on top of SFT?
options: Instead of SFT on a raw base
Only when it beats the SFT checkpoint on the same held-out pairs and does not trip safety/schema kills
why: DPO is optional. A/B it against SFT. A judge that loves length is not a win. DPO-from-base often forgets format.

q: Which task is the strongest RFT candidate?
options: Code that must pass a hidden unit-test suite
why: RFT wants a machine-checkable grader. Tests and schemas qualify. Tone and changing facts do not — use DPO or RAG.

q: A code policy learns to return True from helpers and the reward goes up. What failed?
options: The grader; add those hacks to the suite and bound KL to the SFT reference
why: Reward hacking is the model optimising the grader. A gallery of hacks and a KL bound are the controls, not a smaller rank.

q: Before generating 20k teacher rows you should confirm what?
options: The teacher's terms allow using outputs to train a student
That the student is larger than the teacher
That you have no human set
why: Some APIs forbid training a replacement model. Legal reads the ToS before you generate. Open-weight teachers have licences too.

q: Why distil on production-like prompts rather than only the teacher's demo set?
options: Demos always cover mobile short prompts
On-policy inputs match real traffic; demo-only students fail unseen slices
It reduces licence risk to zero
It removes the need to filter
why: A student trained on polished demos misses short or ugly live prompts. Sample traffic, filter, then train. Demos can seed; they cannot be the whole set.

q: Overall +3, payments slice −8 on the held-out set. Decision?
options: Block: the critical slice is a kill even when the mean looks good
why: Slice metrics exist so money and safety errors cannot hide in a headline. A pre-written kill should stop the run.

q: A VP wants to waive a safety kill in Slack after a pretty mean score. Response?
options: A waiver is a new signed ADR, not a chat message
why: Kill criteria are written before the run so ugly numbers cannot be story-told into a pass. Waivers need the original signers in writing.

q: A tune works in the trainer notebook and rambles in production. Top suspect?
options: Chat template or stop-token mismatch on the serve path
The eval set is too clean
why: Template mismatch is the classic notebook-vs-prod bug. Golden token-id tests and a staging mismatch drill catch it without a retrain.

q: What three ids belong on every tuned generation trace?
options: Base revision, adapter version, and template hash
why: A virtual name is remapped. Base, adapter and template let you reload the artefact that actually answered.
